'''Andreas Lüttge''' is Professor of Earth Science and Professor of Chemistry at [[Rice University]] in Houston, Texas (USA). He was also director of the [[National Corrosion Center]] (NCC) until 2010.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://nationalcorrosioncenter.org/2009/07/dr-andreas-luttge-appointed-director-of-ncc/ |title=Dr. Andreas Lüttge |accessdate=2010-04-20 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20110727111854/http://nationalcorrosioncenter.org/2009/07/dr-andreas-luttge-appointed-director-of-ncc/ |archivedate=2011-07-27 }}</ref> The primary concerns of his research are surface chemical processes at minerals and rocks from low-temperature conditions up to the pressure and temperature conditions throughout the Earth's crust.

Andreas Luttge's degrees are a Habilitation [venia legendi] (1995) and a PhD [Dr. rer. nat.] (1990) from the [[University of Tübingen]] (Germany). In 1995 the [[Alexander von Humboldt Foundation]] awarded a [[Feodor Lynen fellowship]] to Andreas Luttge to visit [[Yale University]] and to work with Prof. [[A.C. Lasaga]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://cohesion.rice.edu/naturalsciences/earthscience/facultyDetail.cfm?riceid=1026 | title=Andreas Lüttge &#124; Department of Earth Science &#124; Rice University }}</ref>

Luttge published numerous studies about the surface dynamics of minerals, glasses and metals,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.chem.rice.edu/facultydetail.cfm?RiceID%3D1026 |title=Rice University &#124; Department of Chemistry |accessdate=2010-04-22 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100604221546/http://www.chem.rice.edu/facultydetail.cfm?RiceID=1026 |archivedate=2010-06-04 }}</ref> including investigations of microbial activity at interfaces.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://terra.rice.edu/department/faculty/aluttge/2006/Luttge_article.html |title=Bacteria could power tiny robots &#124; CNET News.com |accessdate=2010-04-22 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100610172812/http://terra.rice.edu/department/faculty/aluttge/2006/Luttge_article.html |archivedate=2010-06-10 }}</ref> He applies various experimental techniques using [[vertical scanning interferometry]], [[electron microscopy]], and [[atomic force microscopy]] and modeling techniques such as Monte Carlo and ab initio methods. Resulting quantitative kinetic rate data are key prerequisites to provide a better understanding of the dynamics governing many geologic and technologic processes.
